content:
Hello, I'm a phd student in number theory and a complete newbie to Lean. I've been thinking about formalizing Katz's theory of rigid local systems (complex and l-adic versions) and contributing it to mathlib. I used AI to produce some Lean code, but I assume that is not good enough for a PR to Mathlib? Where can i find any guidance on how to produce Lean code good enough to contribute to Mathlib? Here's the repo.

https://github.com/yunhaixiang/RigidLocalSystems/

Nowadays anyone can attempt to formalise any paper (whether they understand it or not) by just giving money to a tech company and then asking their top public LLM to do it. Such experiments typically teach nobody anything.

If you want to learn lean you could ask your LLM instead to write you a tutorial focused on your area of mathematical expertise. Or you could do it the old-fashioned way and read #mil .

Yunhai Xiang said:

but I assume that is not good enough for a PR to Mathlib?

Nobody wants to look at some cheap random LLM-code (I don't mean yours is) and judges for you whether it is good enough for Mathlib. Such code can now be generated by anyone anywhere.

Here is the guide for new contributors https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/how-to-contribute.html.
Thanks! I will read this and improve my code.
My only worry tho is if people would be interested in the formalization of this theory? It is a little niche and the only people i know who care about it are me and my advisor.
Well, and Katz, presumably :wink:
Daniel Litt also held a learning seminar about them in 2023: https://www.daniellitt.com/rigid-local-systems/

Definitely people are interested in rigid local systems! Mathlib isn't really interested in AI-generated code by newcomers who don't know how to tidy it up, but if you want to learn something about how to write idiomatic Lean code then you might well find reviewers who are interested.
